title: 2 Chronicles 16:11–14
context: The Chronicler closes Asa’s reign. His acts are recorded in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. In his thirty-ninth year he suffers a severe disease in his feet, yet seeks only physicians rather than the LORD. He dies in his forty-first year and is buried with great honor in a tomb he prepared, with spices and a very great fire. The parallel in 1 Kings 15:23–24 mentions the disease in his feet in old age but not the physicians.

verses.text: Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa’s acts, first and last, are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler refers to a source that recorded his whole reign, including its later years.
verses.reformedNotes: For Reformed readers, “first and last” quietly admits that the reign had a bright start and a darker close. The work cited here has not survived, and the verse functions as the usual regnal summary.

verses.text: In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa was diseased in his feet. His disease was exceedingly great; yet in his disease he didn’t seek the LORD, but just the physicians.
verses.arminianNotes: In his thirty-ninth year Asa suffers a severe disease in his feet, yet seeks only physicians, not the LORD. Arminian readers note that the criticism concerns not seeking God, not the use of physicians as such.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sobering end for a king who once sought God. Shared ground: 1 Kings 15:23 mentions the disease in his feet in old age but not physicians, and both traditions avoid assuming the illness was punishment.

verses.text: Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the forty-first year of his reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa dies in the forty-first year of his reign. Arminian readers note that his long reign included both faithful and unfaithful years, and the Chronicler records both honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s patience with Asa through a reign of mixed faithfulness. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to the forty-one years in 1 Kings 15:10.

verses.text: They buried him in his own tomb, which he had dug out for himself in David’s city, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art; and they made a very great fire for him.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa is buried in his own tomb with spices and a very great fire. Arminian readers note the honor given to him by the people, despite the failures of his final years.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the great fire was likely a burning of spices in his honor rather than cremation (compare Jeremiah 34:5). Shared ground: both traditions read the burial as a sign of the respect in which Asa was held.
